title: Why the Sound stays cold in July
teaches: Salt and density, the two-layer exchange over the sills, renewal at neap tides, upwelling, and the salt wedge at a river mouth
summary: **Salt makes water heavy.** Sea water in the Sound is about 2 to 3 percent denser than river water, far more than any change of temperature makes, so salt sets the layers.
**The Sound runs as two layers.** Fresher water flows out toward the Strait on top, and salty ocean water flows in underneath to replace the salt it carries away.
**A little river water drives a lot of exchange.** Each cubic metre of river water draws in something like twenty of ocean water below.
**The sills stir the layers.** Tidal currents over the shallow rise at Admiralty Inlet churn the water top to bottom, and much of the water leaving on top is mixed down and carried back in.
**Deep water is renewed at neap tides.** When the tide is weak, less fresh water is mixed into the inflow, so it is dense enough to sink to the bottom of the Main Basin.
**The summer inflow is cold.** Northerly winds on the outer coast bring cold deep water up along the shore, and that water feeds the Strait's deep inflow.
**Stirring spreads the sun's heat through the whole depth.** That, with the cold supply, keeps the Main Basin near 12 to 14 °C in summer, while shallow South Sound inlets reach 18 to 20 °C.
**A salt wedge belongs to a narrow river mouth.** Where little stirs the layers, salt water creeps upstream along the bottom until the river's flow holds it back.
**The Ballard Locks keep the salt out of Lake Union.** Salt water that gets through with each opening slides along the canal bed and is caught by a drain.

blocks.text: On a hot afternoon in late July, wade into Lake Washington at Madison Park and the water is warm enough to swim in for an hour; lesson 6 found its surface above 20 °C. Drive fifteen minutes west to Golden Gardens or Alki and walk into the Sound, and your ankles ache. The water there is about 12 or 13 °C. The same sun shines on both, through the same air, and the Sound has had all of May, June and July to warm up.

Lesson 6 explained a lake that stays cold at the bottom: warm water floats on cold, the layers hold apart all summer, and the sun's heat stays near the top. The Sound is cold at the top as well as the bottom. Something takes the summer's heat away, or brings cold water in to replace it, or both.

The first good look at the Sound's depths came from the United States Exploring Expedition under Lieutenant Charles Wilkes, whose boats spent the summer of 1841 charting the Sound with the lead line, a weight on a marked rope dropped to the bottom. The charts that followed, and every chart since, show a sea much deeper than a river valley: long basins more than 200 metres deep in places, the deepest near 280 metres, each cut off from the next by a shallower rise in the floor at its entrance. Those rises, the **sills** of lesson 11, and the depth behind them, are where the answer lies.[^wilkes]

Lesson 6 built the idea of **density**, how much a given volume of water weighs, from temperature: cold fresh water is heavier than warm, so it sinks. Salt does the same job, and does it far more strongly. Water in the Sound holds about 30 grams of dissolved salt in every kilogram, a little less than the open ocean's 35. That salt makes it about 2 to 3 percent denser than river water: a cubic metre of Sound water weighs about 1,023 kilograms, a cubic metre of river water about 1,000.

Two or three percent sounds small until you compare it with temperature. Warming fresh water from 4 °C to 20 °C makes it less than 0.2 percent lighter.[^density] So in the Sound salt decides which water floats and which sinks, and temperature has only a small say. A layer of fresher water from the rivers will float on salty water even if the fresher water is the colder of the two.

**In the kitchen.** Fill a clear glass halfway with tap water. In a cup, stir two teaspoons of salt into some water and add a few drops of food colouring. Pour the coloured salt water very slowly down the side of the glass, or through a straw held to the bottom. It slides under the tap water and stays there as a layer, with a sharp boundary you can see through the side.

Rivers pour fresh water into the Sound all year: the Skagit, by far the largest, then the Snohomish, the Puyallup, the Nisqually and dozens more. That water is light, so it spreads over the surface and flows seaward on top, out through Admiralty Inlet toward the Strait of Juan de Fuca. On the way it mixes with the salt water beneath and carries some of that salt out with it.

Salt is leaving the Sound all the time, then, yet the Sound stays salty. Something must bring the salt back. It is ocean water, flowing in along the bottom, under the outgoing layer, from the Strait. This is the **two-layer exchange**: fresher water out on top, salty water in below, one on top of the other and moving in opposite directions, while the tide sloshes both back and forth twice a day. Oceanographers call a body of water that works this way an **estuary**, and by that definition the whole Sound is one.

**An estimate** of how much ocean water the river water draws in. Salt is neither made nor lost, so the salt carried in below must equal the salt carried out on top. Suppose the deep inflow holds about 31 grams of salt per kilogram and the surface outflow about 29.5. Each cubic metre of outflow is a cubic metre of inflow plus the river water mixed into it, and the salt must balance, so the inflow must be about 29.5 ÷ (31 − 29.5), roughly 20 times the river flow. A modest amount of river water drives an exchange twenty times larger.[^knudsen]

The biggest river of all doesn't enter the Sound. The Fraser, which drains much of interior British Columbia, reaches the sea at Vancouver and brings more fresh water on average than all of Puget Sound's rivers together, with a great flood of snowmelt from late May into July. Its water spreads across the Strait of Georgia and works south and west through the San Juan Islands to the Strait of Juan de Fuca. No one in Seattle sees the Fraser's water as such, but it freshens the whole system, and some of it, well mixed, comes back into the Sound in the deep inflow.

blocks.caption: The Salish Sea's two-layer exchange. Fresher water leaves the Sound on top (blue) and ocean water comes in below (dark blue); in summer the coast's upwelling (pale) supplies the cold deep water.

blocks.text: If that were all, the Sound would be layered like a summer lake: a warm, fresh skin on top and cold salt water below, holding apart. It isn't, because of the sills. The floor of Admiralty Inlet rises to a sill only about 60 metres down, between the deep water of the Strait and the deep Main Basin behind it. Twice a day the tide drags the whole column of water over that rise at a few knots (lesson 11), and the water tumbles and churns as it goes. The two layers are stirred into each other. Tacoma Narrows, at the entrance to South Sound, does the same.

Much of the fresher water heading out on top never makes it to the Strait. It is mixed down at the sill into the salty water below and carried straight back into the Sound with the inflow. Oceanographers call this **reflux**, and their estimates for Admiralty Inlet put it at roughly half or more of the outflowing water.

Stirring is also what keeps the surface cold. **An estimate.** In July the sun delivers about 250 watts on each square metre of the Sound, averaged over day and night. Over a week that is about 150 million joules on each square metre. Warming a cubic metre of water by one degree takes about 4 million joules. Kept in the top 5 metres, as in a calm lake, a week of sunshine could warm that layer by about 7 °C, before counting the heat lost at night. Stir the same heat through the hundred metres or more that the sills mix, and the whole column warms by less than half a degree. The sill takes the summer's heat and spreads it so thin that the surface never gets the chance to warm the way a lake does.

The deep water of the Main Basin is replaced from time to time by new water from the Strait. The new water has to be heavy enough to sink all the way to the bottom, and whether it is depends on how much fresher water the sill has mixed into it on the way in. In a study published in 1982, W. Rockwell Geyer and Glenn Cannon showed from measurements at the sill and in the basin that the new deep water arrives in pulses, about twice a month. The figure is a model of what they found. Before you play it, guess when the pulses come.

blocks.caption: A month of exchange at the Admiralty Inlet sill. A model: salt alone sets the density, and the mixing at the sill grows with the strength of the tidal current.
blocks.task: Guess, then play at least past day 15

blocks.text: The pulses come at **neap tides**, the weak tides of lesson 8, and stop at springs. It seems backward at first: the strong tides move the most water, so surely they should deliver the most. But at springs the fast currents over the sill stir hard, much of the outgoing fresher water is mixed into the inflow, and the inflow arrives lighter than the water already at the bottom of the basin. It can't sink through heavier water, so it spreads out at the depth where it fits, partway down. At neaps the stirring slackens, the inflow keeps more of its salt, and it is the heaviest water around. It slides down the far side of the sill and along the floor of the basin, lifting the older bottom water ahead of it.

Move the river slider and the details shift: more river water makes the surface layer fresher, the inflow a little lighter and the whole Sound a little less salty. The rhythm stays the same. Renewal follows the Moon's cycle of springs and neaps, not the rivers.

Stirring explains why the summer's heat spreads thin. The other half of the answer is what comes in. In spring and summer the winds along the outer coast of Washington blow mostly from the north. Because of the Earth's spin, the surface water they push is turned to its right, which here is offshore, away from the coast.[^ekman] Water from below rises to take its place: cold, salty water from a hundred metres or more down, rich in the nutrients that sank there over the years. This is **upwelling**, and it can make the coastal water as cold in August as in February.

That upwelled water is the deep water that flows in along the bottom of the Strait of Juan de Fuca. All summer, the two-layer exchange draws cold ocean water from the coast into the Sound, while the sills stir it up to the surface. The cold you feel at Alki in July is partly water that was a hundred metres down off the outer coast not long before. The nutrients it carries also feed the plankton that turn the summer Sound green, which is the next course's story.

The Sound is not cold everywhere. The cold depends on the stirring and the supply, and where both are weak the water warms. The long, shallow inlets of South Sound, Budd Inlet, Eld Inlet, Totten and Hammersley, lie far beyond Tacoma Narrows at the very end of the exchange, and in a warm summer their surface water reaches 18 to 20 °C. Hood Canal, a long dead end with weak tidal currents, layers in summer much as a lake does, with warm water on top; lesson 13 follows what happens beneath.

blocks.caption: Typical surface temperatures on a summer afternoon, rounded. Each varies from year to year and day to day.

parts.title: A wedge in the river mouth

blocks.text: The two layers can hold apart where little stirs them. At the mouth of a river that enters through a narrow, dredged channel, the Duwamish Waterway through Seattle's industrial district for one, salt water pushes upstream along the bottom as a thin, tapering layer under the fresh water flowing out on top. Its front, the toe, can be several kilometres from the mouth. This is a **salt wedge**. The heavy salt water would creep all the way upstream if nothing held it back; what holds it back is the river, dragging on the top of the wedge as it flows out over it. A strong river pushes the wedge back toward the sea, and a weak one lets it in.

blocks.caption: A salt wedge in a river channel 10 metres deep, held back by the river's flow. A model of a wedge with no tide; a real wedge also moves in and out with the tide.
blocks.task: Find a flow that lets the salt reach 6 km upstream, and a flood that pushes it back within 1 km

blocks.text: The best-known wedge in Seattle is one people made. The Ballard Locks, opened in 1917, lift ships from the salt water of Salmon Bay to the fresh water of the Lake Washington Ship Canal and Lake Union. Every time the large lock opens to the canal it lets out a lock full of salt water, which slides along the canal bed toward Lake Union like a wedge with nothing to stop it. Left alone, the salt would build up in the bottom of Lake Union and beyond. The engineers' answer uses the same physics as the glass in the kitchen: salt water lies on the bottom, so it can be caught there. A barrier on the floor of the large lock holds much of it back, and a drain in the canal bed just above the locks collects the salt water that gets past and returns it below the dam. The Seattle branch (S2) tells the story of the locks.

blocks.caption: The Ballard Locks from the side, not to scale. Salt water that gets past the large lock slides along the bottom of the canal and is caught by a drain.

blocks.text: The boundary between the two layers carries waves of its own, called **internal waves**. Because the two layers differ in density by only a few percent, gravity's pull back toward level is weak, and these waves are slow and can be tall, rising and falling many metres inside the water while the surface above barely moves. The tide flowing over the sills makes them, and they march across the Main Basin and through Admiralty Inlet in groups.

You can see them without seeing them. On a calm day, look out over the Sound from a ferry or a high bluff and you may see long, smooth bands lying across the rippled water, parallel to one another and sometimes a few hundred metres apart. Each band is a **slick**, where the internal wave below pulls the surface water together and gathers the thin natural films on it, which smooth the ripples. The slicks drift along with the waves underneath.

blocks.caption: Six questions on the Sound's layers
blocks.task: Choose the best answer to each

items.ask: Why does river water spread over the top of the salt water in Puget Sound?
choices: It holds less salt, so it is lighter, by more than any difference in temperature
It is warmer than the Sound, and warm water always floats on cold
It arrives moving faster than the Sound's water, so it rides over it
items.why: Sea water in the Sound is 2 to 3 percent denser than river water, while temperature changes density by only a few tenths of a percent.

items.ask: Why does ocean water flow into Puget Sound along the bottom all year?
choices: The fresher surface water carries salt out, and salty water from below must replace it
The Sound's floor slopes downhill from the Strait, so heavy water runs in by gravity alone
The flood tide is always stronger near the bottom than the ebb tide is
items.why: Outflow on top takes salt away; the salt balance is kept by an inflow of salty water underneath, many times the rivers' flow.

items.ask: What is reflux at the Admiralty Inlet sill?
choices: Outflowing surface water mixed down at the sill and carried back into the Sound
Tide water that bounces back from the southern end of the Sound
River water that flows upstream on the flood tide
items.why: Tidal stirring over the sill mixes the layers, so much of the water leaving on top is returned in the inflow below.

items.ask: Why does new deep water reach the bottom of the Main Basin at neap tides rather than spring tides?
choices: Weak neap currents mix less fresher water into the inflow, so it stays dense enough to sink
Neap tides carry more water over the sill than spring tides do
The rivers run lower at neap tides, so the inflow is saltier
items.why: At springs hard stirring lightens the inflow so it spreads at mid-depth; at neaps it keeps its salt and sinks to the floor.

items.ask: Which best explains why the Main Basin stays near 12 to 14 °C in summer?
choices: Stirring at the sills spreads the sun's heat through deep water, and cold upwelled ocean water keeps flowing in
The Sound is too deep for sunlight to reach most of its water
Cold river water from melting snow fills the Sound each summer
items.why: The sun's heat is mixed through a hundred metres or more, and the summer inflow is cold water brought up along the coast by north winds.

items.ask: In a river mouth with a salt wedge, what happens to the wedge when the river floods?
choices: It is pushed back toward the sea, because the stronger flow drags harder on it
It moves further upstream, because the flood brings more salt
It stays where it is, because the salt water is heavier than the river
items.why: The wedge creeps upstream along the bottom until the river's drag on it holds it back; a stronger river holds it nearer the mouth.

wilkes.title: Wilkes's names
wilkes.text: Wilkes's expedition named many places on the Sound that still carry the names, among them Elliott Bay, Commencement Bay and Maury Island. The expedition had sailed from Virginia in 1838 and spent four years at sea; its Pacific Northwest survey took up the summer of 1841.

knudsen.title: Knudsen's balance
knudsen.text: The Danish oceanographer Martin Knudsen wrote down this salt and water balance in 1900, for the Baltic. It gives the size of an estuary's exchange from two salinities and the river flow, without measuring the currents at all.

ekman.title: Turned to the right
ekman.text: In the Northern Hemisphere the Earth's spin turns moving water to the right. Averaged through the wind-driven surface layer, the water moves at right angles to the wind, as Vagn Walfrid Ekman worked out in 1905. A north wind on the Washington coast blows toward the south, so the water moves west, out to sea.

density.title: Salt and temperature together
density.text: Sea water's density depends on salt, temperature and pressure together. Near the Sound's temperatures each extra gram of salt per kilogram adds about 0.8 kilograms to a cubic metre, while each degree of warming takes off only about 0.15. The figures here use salt alone.
